x: The dashboards are green. CPU sits at 55%, memory is fine, the database looks bored. And p99 has just gone from 180 ms to 4 seconds. Someone in the incident channel types the sentence that has burned more engineering hours than any bug: "Let's just double the connection pool and see." Sometimes that works. More often it moves the queue somewhere else and the tail gets worse. My rule is blunt: no change goes in until you can name the saturated resource and show the number that proves it. Here is the method behind that rule. Every system has a throughput ceiling set by its most constrained resource. The operational laws make this concrete: Utilisation Law: U = X × D, where X is throughput and D is the service demand (the total busy time one request needs from that resource). Bottleneck bound: X_max = capacity / D_max. The resource with the largest demand relative to its capacity caps the whole system. A worked example. Say each request costs 20 ms of CPU in the API tier, which runs 3 pods with 2 cores each, and 8 ms of CPU on a database with 8 cores. Tier Capacity Demand per request Max throughput API 6 cores 0.020 core-s 6 / 0.020 = 300 req/s Database 8 cores 0.008 core-s 8 / 0.008 = 1,000 req/s The API tier caps the system at 300 req/s. Tuning the database here buys nothing. At 240 req/s the API tier sits at U = 240 × 0.020 / 6 = 0.8, which is already where queueing delay starts to bite. It falls over, and takes the application with it. The cache was never just an optimisation. It had quietly become a load-bearing wall. The caching pattern you choose decides how you fail, and at scale the failures that matter are not "the cache is a bit slow" but sudden shifts of load onto the system the cache was protecting. Thirty seconds later the origin, which normally serves 500 requests a second, is taking 10,000. The site goes down in the one hour it most needed to stay up. Nothing was broken. The CDN did exactly what it was told. Most teams treat the CDN as a box that makes static files fast. From a performance engineering point of view it is the first tier of your capacity model . It decides how much traffic your origin sees, and it fails in ways that stay invisible until a busy day. Origin request rate = edge request rate × (1 − hit ratio). t: Your load test is lying about p99
d: A closed-loop load tool waits when the system stalls, so the worst requests are never measured. How to spot coordinated omission and fix it.
h: How to spot it in results you already have
Open models have a cost: plan for it
Need this done on your project?
x: Your load test report says p99 is 1 ms. Clean run, green thresholds, ready for sign-off. During that same run, the service froze for 10 seconds. The real p99 was about 9 seconds. The tool didn't lie on purpose. It simply stopped asking questions at the exact moment the answers got bad. That is coordinated omission , a term from Gil Tene, and it is sitting quietly in a lot of load test reports right now. It doesn't make results a little optimistic. It can understate tail latency by several orders of magnitude. Most load tools default to a closed model : each virtual user sends a request, waits for the response, optionally thinks, then sends the next one. That works until the system stalls. When the server freezes for two seconds (a GC pause, a lock, a failover), every virtual user is stuck waiting on one request. During those two seconds, the requests a real user population would have sent are never sent. The tool records one slow sample per user, not the hundreds of slow experiences real users would have had. The tool has "coordinated" with the system, and the omitted samples are exactly the bad ones. Real users do not coordinate. They arrive whenever they arrive, whether or not your service is mid-pause. That is an open model : arrivals are independent of response times. Imagine one closed-loop thread intended to send a request every 10 ms (100 req/s) for 100 seconds: 10,000 requests in total. Then the p99.9 SLO breaches again, and the slow requests line up with GC events. Someone drops MaxGCPauseMillis to 50. The tail gets worse. The pause goal was never the right number to watch. It limits how long each pause is. Tail latency depends on how many requests a pause lands on. A request is hurt by GC if a stop-the-world pause starts while it is in flight, or if it arrives during one. With pause frequency f, pause length p and request duration d, the share of requests that overlap a pause is roughly: overlap ≈ f × (p + d) This holds while the result is small. For example: 1 young GC per second, 25 ms pauses and 40 ms requests. Overlap ≈ 1 × (0.025 + 0.040) = 6.5% of requests . GC time is only 2.5% of wall-clock time, which looks harmless on a throughput dashboard. Yet GC sits inside your p95, so it certainly defines p99 and p99.9. Every pause met the goal. Frequency is mostly allocation rate divided by eden size. Eden is the part of the young generation where new objects are allocated. At 1 GB/s into a 1 GB eden, you get roughly one young GC per second. Length is mostly driven by live data, not garbage. A young collection copies surviving objects and scans roots (thread stacks and, in G1, remembered sets that track old-to-young references). Dead objects cost almost nothing to reclaim. Need this done on your project?
x: The load test passed. p99 was 120 ms at twice the expected peak, and everyone signed off. A week after launch, the same endpoint sits at 4 seconds p99 during the evening rush. You open the slow query log and it is almost empty. Nothing in the database looks slow. Yet the database is the reason. Most database bottlenecks that escape load testing are not slow queries. They are waits : for a pooled connection, for a lock, for many small round trips. A typical test environment removes the conditions that create those waits: A small dataset. The whole database fits in shared_buffers , so every read is a cache hit, and the planner happily chooses plans that only work on small tables. Uniform parameters. The script picks customer IDs from a flat list. Production has a few customers with a million orders each. No concurrent writers. Batch jobs and other services that update the same rows are absent. No replicas. Reads go to the primary, so replica lag and read-after-write anomalies never appear. Test with production-like volume and skew, then check in this order. This is the one that hides best. When every connection in the application's pool is in use, new requests queue inside the application for a free one. That time counts in your response time but never in pg_stat_statements , because no query is running. t: Why 500 threads made it slower
d: Size thread pools with Little's Law and the wait-to-compute ratio, bound queues by your latency budget, and see what virtual threads change.
h: Little's Law gives you the floor
CPU-bound vs I/O-bound: the wait-to-compute ratio
Queue choice changes behaviour, not just capacity
Web server defaults are not sizing
Reading a thread dump for saturation
Need this done on your project?
x: Traffic climbs, latency follows. Someone opens the config, finds maxThreads: 200 , and says the obvious thing: "Make it 500, to be safe." The deploy goes out and p99 gets worse . CPU has barely moved. A thread dump shows hundreds of threads parked, all waiting for one of 10 database connections. A thread pool is a queueing system: a fixed number of servers (threads) in front of a queue. That means it can be sized with arithmetic instead of folklore, and its failure modes can be predicted before they page you. Little's Law : L = λ × W. The average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends in it. For a thread pool, L is the number of busy threads, λ is throughput, and W is how long a request holds a thread (not end-to-end latency, which also includes time queued). Say an endpoint serves 400 req/s and each request holds a thread for 50 ms: L = 400 × 0.05 = 20 busy threads on average. That is the average, not the size. Arrivals are bursty and service times have a tail, so the pool needs headroom above it, and the queue absorbs short bursts. But it tells you instantly that a pool of 500 for this workload is 25× the average need. For CPU-bound work (parsing, compression, crypto), more threads than cores only adds context switching. Use roughly the number of cores available to the process. For work that mostly waits (database calls, HTTP calls), Brian Goetz's formula in Java Concurrency in Practice gives the starting point: N_threads

d: Why response time climbs long before 100% utilisation, how Kingman's formula prices bursty traffic, and why constant-rate load tests miss it.
h: Kingman: variability multiplies the wait, not the work
One server or many changes the answer
Load test with the burstiness you will get
Need this done on your project?
x: Your load test holds 1,200 req/s with a steady 5 ms p99. Production averages the same 1,200 req/s, and twice an hour the same endpoint spikes to 2 seconds. Nobody changed the code. The CPU graph says 65%. The test and production differ in something the dashboard doesn't show: variability. The test sent requests at a perfectly even rate. Production arrives in clumps, and for a few minutes at a time it runs much hotter than the hourly average suggests. Queueing theory predicts exactly this, and it gives you numbers you can plan with. Start with the simplest model, M/M/1 : Poisson arrivals, exponentially distributed service times, one server with one queue. Utilisation is U = λ × S, the arrival rate times the mean service time. Mean response time is R = S / (1 − U), of which the time spent waiting in the queue is Wq = U / (1 − U) × S. With S = 10 ms: Utilisation M/M/1 response time Constant-rate test (Ca = 0) Bursty arrivals (Ca = 2) 50% 20 ms 15 ms 35 ms 70% 33 ms 22 ms 68 ms 80% 50 ms 30 ms 110 ms 90% 100 ms 55 ms 235 ms 95% 200 ms 105 ms 485 ms (The last two columns assume Cs = 1 and come from Kingman's formula below.) There is no sharp corner in the maths. The curve is a hyperbola, and its slope is S / (1 − U)². At 80% each extra percentage point of utilisation adds about 2.5 ms. At 90% it adds 10 ms. d: HPA scale-out lag is metric delay, sync period, node provisioning and pod start stacked together. What the stabilisation window really does.
h: Stabilisation windows slow scale-down, not scale-up
The cost of lag, in requests
Fixes, in the order I'd try them

x: Traffic triples in a minute. Your HPA notices, does the maths and asks for 60 more pods. Then nothing happens. For the next three minutes the existing 25 pods take the whole surge, queues fill and p99 climbs past your client timeout. When the new pods finally go Ready, the incident is already over and the HPA gets the blame. Someone shortens the 5-minute stabilisation window. Nothing improves, because that window was never in the way. The HPA's decision is the fast part. The lag lives in the chain around it. Every sync period (15 s by default, set by --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period on kube-controller-manager) the controller computes: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue) If the ratio is within a tolerance of 10% (default), it does nothing. Three details matter more than the formula: CPU utilisation is relative to the pod's CPU request , not the node or the limit. Requests set too high make the HPA react late. Requests set too low make it scale on noise. Pods that are not yet Ready are treated as using 0% of the target when the controller computes a scale-up. This deliberately damps the next step while earlier pods are still starting. A saturated pod cannot report demand it never received. If the work is CPU-bound and pods are pinned, measured utilisation stops at the ceiling while real demand keeps rising, so each sync under-asks. Somewhere between them sat a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, a CDN that missed its cache and went back to the origin in Sydney, and twelve round trips that could have been three. "It's the network" is usually true, and rarely specific enough to fix. Bandwidth is how much data per second the pipe carries. Latency is how long one round trip takes. For typical API calls and web pages, latency dominates: a 20 KB JSON response takes about 0.2 ms to transmit at 1 Gbit/s, but each round trip between Melbourne and Singapore is roughly 80 to 100 ms, and light in fibre can't do much better. That is why the number of round trips matters more than payload size for small requests. Larger responses add more round trips while TCP's congestion window grows (slow start), which is why the first 14 KB or so of a response is cheap and the next few hundred KB on a fresh connection are not. x: Guides · Gatling · Injection profiles You set atOnceUsers(1000) to simulate "1,000 users". The test fires 1,000 journeys in the same millisecond, the server queues them all, and the report shows a spike nobody will ever see in production. The injection profile is your workload model, so it has to match how real traffic arrives. On this page Open vs closed in Gatling Open injection steps Closed injection steps Both in one simulation Finding capacity with incrementUsersPerSec Throttling and pacing Gatling makes you choose explicitly: injectOpen(...) or injectClosed(...) . You can't mix open and closed steps for one scenario. Open : you control the arrival rate of new users. Each user runs the scenario and leaves. If the system slows down, users pile up inside it, as on a real public website. Use it when you have a throughput target. Closed : you control how many users are active at once. A new user starts only when one finishes. Use it when the real population is fixed: a call centre, a pool of workers, a ticket queue that admits N people at a time. A closed model under-reports latency when the system struggles, because it sends less work exactly then. That's coordinated omission . The background is in the open vs closed workload model glossary entry and the load profiles explainer . Step Does nothingFor(d) Wait atOnceUsers(n) n users at the same moment. Every login returns 200, every "add to basket" returns 403, and the response body says "invalid CSRF token". The script is replaying a value the server issued once, during recording. Correlation fixes that: capture the value from a response, then send it back on the next request. Correlation means any value the server generates that the client must send back: session IDs, CSRF or anti-forgery tokens, OAuth state and code , order and basket IDs, pagination cursors, ASP.NET __VIEWSTATE , signed URLs. The reliable way to find them: Record the same flow twice (two logins, two orders). Diff the two recordings. Any request parameter, header or path segment that differs is either dynamic data from the server (correlate it) or data you chose ( parameterise it). For each dynamic value, search the earlier responses for where it first appears. That response is where the extractor goes. Cookies are the exception. The HTTP Cookie Manager handles Set-Cookie automatically, so do not extract session cookies by hand unless the app copies them into a header or body. All extractors are Post Processors: right-click the sampler whose response contains the value, then Add → Post Processors . Put the extractor as a child of that one sampler. Each thread fires the next request the instant the last one returns, so 50 "users" generate 2,000 requests per second. That can be more traffic than your real peak of 20,000 users ever produces. Or you add think time and the rate collapses the moment the server slows down. Timers decide what load you are really applying. A timer runs before each sampler in its scope. Its delay is not included in the sample's response time. A timer at Thread Group level applies to every sampler in the group. Ten samplers means ten pauses per iteration. Several timers in the same scope add up . A Constant Timer of 1 s plus a Uniform Random Timer of 0–2 s gives 1–3 s before each sampler. To pause before one sampler only, make the timer its child. To pause after a step, add a Flow Control Action sampler (Logical action: Pause, Duration 0) and put the timer under it. Flow Control Action does not write a sample to the results. Model think time where a real user pauses: after a page loads and before the next click. API calls a browser fires together with no pause between them should have no timer between them. On this page Open vs closed: the one decision that matters Every executor, and when to use it Arrival-rate maths: sizing preAllocatedVUs dropped_iterations: when k6 can't keep up A mixed workload with several scenarios Scenario options you will need In a closed model a fixed number of users loop: send a request, wait for the response, think, repeat. When the server slows down, every user waits longer, so the request rate falls. The test quietly backs off at the exact moment the system is struggling. In an open model new work arrives on a schedule whether or not earlier requests finished, like real visitors on a public site. When the server slows down, requests pile up and queues grow, which is what actually happens in production. The closed model's backing off has a name: coordinated omission . The tool coordinates with the problem and never sends the requests that would have been slow, so your p99 looks better than reality. The percentiles explainer shows it happening. My rule: use an arrival-rate (open) executor when you have a throughput target , such as "500 checkouts a minute" or "2,000 requests a second at peak". x: Guides · LoadRunner · Correlation Your script replays fine at 4 pm. At 9 am the next day every vuser fails at step three with "invalid request". Nothing in the application changed. The script is sending a session token, a CSRF value and a basket ID that were valid yesterday. Correlation means capturing those server-generated values at run time and sending back the fresh ones. A value needs correlating when the server generates it and the client sends it back later. Typical suspects: Session IDs in URLs or form fields (cookies are handled automatically by the Web protocol, as long as you don't clear them mid-journey) CSRF and anti-forgery tokens, __VIEWSTATE and __EVENTVALIDATION in ASP.NET Web Forms OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens and authorisation codes IDs created during the journey: order, basket, quote, policy, payment intent Timestamps and nonces the server echoes and validates The quickest way to find them: record the same journey twice, compare the two scripts, and look at every long or random-looking value that differs. Then search each value in the earlier server responses (the Snapshot view or the recording log) to find where it first appears. That response is where the capture goes. The workhorse. x: Guides · Locust · CI and reports Locust in CI either fails on every single error, including the one timeout in 50,000 requests, or never fails at all. Neither is useful. What you want is a budget: p95 under a limit and failures under a rate, the same way you'd write an SLO. On this page What Locust does by default A pass/fail budget with an event listener CSV, HTML and JSON reports GitHub Actions Making CI results trustworthy A headless run exits with code 1 if any request failed, and 0 otherwise. Locust has no built-in latency budget. Locust fires a quitting event just before it exits. A listener can read the final statistics and set environment.process_exit_code , which replaces the default: import logging from locust import HttpUser, task, constant, events class ApiUser(HttpUser): wait_time = constant(1) @task def browse(self): self.client.get("/products") @events.quitting.add_listener def enforce_budget(environment, **kwargs): """Set the process exit code from the results, so CI fails on a breach.""" stats = environment.stats.total p95 = stats.get_response_time_percentile(0.95) if stats.num_requests == 0: logging.error("No requests were made") environment.process_exit_code = 1 elif stats.fail_ratio > 0.01: logging.error(f"Failed: {stats.fail_ratio:.2%} of requests failed (budget 1%)") environment.process_exit

Two weeks later production users complain about 6-second transfers at lunchtime. The SLA was an average over the whole test, including the ramp-up, and the slow minutes were averaged away. NeoLoad gives you per-interval SLAs, percentiles and comparisons. Use them, and decide what "pass" means before the run. Did the load run as designed? Users over time matched the scenario, and throughput (transactions or requests per second) reached the target. If throughput flattened while users kept rising, that is your first finding. Did it work? Error count and rate, which requests failed and with what. A run with 8% errors has different response times from the one you planned. Were the generators healthy? Check the load generators' CPU and memory in the monitors. A saturated generator adds its own delay. Only then: how fast? Percentiles per transaction in the steady state. The Results section of the desktop app holds every run of the project. By the time a slow endpoint is found, it is buried under 20 merges. NeoLoad's as-code YAML and the neoload command line let a pipeline upload a project, run it on a zone in NeoLoad Web and fail the build on SLAs, without anyone opening the GUI. A NeoLoad project can be written as YAML: servers, variables, User Paths, populations, scenarios and SLA profiles. The schema is documented in Tricentis's neoload-models repository on GitHub and in the NeoLoad docs ("YAML format"). Files must end in .yaml or .yml . h: NeoLoad correlation: trust the wizard, then check its work
x: Guides · NeoLoad · Correlation and variables The post-recording wizard found 14 dynamic parameters and the User Path check is green. You run 200 users and 30% of them fail at payment. The wizard correlated the session token and the CSRF value, but the basket ID comes back in a JSON response it treated as static, and every user is paying for the same basket. Automatic correlation gets you most of the way. The rest is knowing where to look. A dynamic parameter is a value the server generates and the client sends back later: session IDs, CSRF tokens, OAuth tokens, IDs created during the journey. NeoLoad handles them two ways: Framework dynamic parameters : predefined rules for known frameworks and applications. NeoLoad ships frameworks for common platforms, including a SAP Fiori framework added in 2026.2. Generic dynamic parameters : detected by comparing values across requests and responses, then configured automatically. The post-recording wizard runs a dynamic parameter search for you. You can run it again from the User Path at any time, which is worth doing after you fix a correlation, because a broken early value can hide later ones. When the search misses something, add a variable extractor on the request whose response contains the value (select the request, open its advanced settings and the Variable extractors tab). The main fields: Field Meaning Variable name Use it later as ${basketId} Extract from Body, headers or both. Narrower is safer Starting with / Ending with T

h: NeoLoad scenarios: from "500 users" to a workload
Not sure your scenario models production?
x: Guides · NeoLoad · Populations and scenarios The brief says "test with 500 users". You put one User Path in a population, set a constant load of 500 for an hour, and press Run. Every user starts in the first second, logs in at once, and the authentication service falls over in a way it never does in production. A scenario is where you turn a headline number into a mix of journeys, a rate and a shape over time. A population is a group of User Paths with a percentage each, adding up to 100%. For example, a "Retail banking" population might be 60% Check balance, 25% Transfer and 15% Pay bill. Build the percentages from production analytics, not guesses. See workload model . populations: - name: RetailBanking user_paths: - name: CheckBalance distribution: 60% - name: Transfer distribution: 25% - name: PayBill distribution: 15% Use separate populations when journeys need different load shapes: steady browsing traffic in one, a batch-like burst of statement downloads in another. Each population in a scenario gets its own load policy. In the Runtime section, a scenario lists populations, each with one load policy: Policy Shape Use it for Constant A fixed number of users, optionally started gradually with a ramp-up delay Steady-state load and soak tests Ramp-up Start with N users and add M every interval, up to an optional maximum Finding where response times bend, step tests, breakpoint tests Peaks Alternate between a minimum and maximum phase Checking the system recovers after peak

5. Think time and pacing in the User Path
User Path that passes but doesn't feel right?
x: Guides · NeoLoad · User Paths and recording NeoLoad records a journey in two minutes and the post-recording wizard correlates most of it for you. That speed is the tool's selling point, and also the trap. A recorded User Path with the login in the wrong container, no transactions and no content checks will run beautifully and tell you very little. Here is how to structure one so the results mean something. Every User Path has three top-level containers: Container Runs Put here Init Once per virtual user, at start Log in, if real users stay logged in across many actions Actions Repeatedly, once per iteration The journey you are measuring End Once per virtual user, at stop Log out, clean up Where the login goes is a workload decision. If each real session is "log in, check balance, log out", record all of it into Actions, otherwise the authentication service is barely tested. LoadRunner users will recognise the pattern: it maps directly to vuser_init , Action and vuser_end . Each User Path also has a user session setting (reset cookies and cache between iterations or not). Match it to how real users behave: a new session per iteration for "log in, do one thing, leave" journeys, a kept session when one virtual user is one long-lived user. Start recording from the toolbar, choose the User Path and the container to record into, and NeoLoad opens a browser routed through its recording proxy. x: Guides · Specialist topics · Chaos and resilience The architecture diagram has retries, a circuit breaker, a fallback cache and two availability zones. Nobody has seen any of them work. Then the payment provider slows from 200 ms to 4 seconds at 8 pm on a Friday. Retries triple the traffic to it, every request thread waits on it, and the whole site goes down because one optional dependency got slow. Resilience you haven't tested is a hope, not a feature. Chaos engineering grew out of Netflix's practice of deliberately breaking parts of its production system (Chaos Monkey). The published principles boil down to this: Define steady state as a measurable output: orders per minute, p95 latency, error rate. Not CPU. Write a hypothesis: "If one of three payment pods is killed, checkout success stays above 99.5% and p95 stays under 1 second." Inject real-world events: instance loss, latency, errors from dependencies, network partitions, full disks, clock skew. Minimise the blast radius: start small (one pod, a small share of traffic, a test environment) and have a way to stop at once. Automate and repeat: resilience decays as the system changes. An experiment that passed in March proves little in November. An experiment that disproves the hypothesis is a success: you found a weakness before your users did. x: Guides · Specialist topics · Microservices and cloud "It autoscales" is the most expensive sentence in cloud performance. The traffic spike arrives in 40 seconds. The metrics notice after 30, the autoscaler decides after 15 more, new pods wait 2 minutes for a node, then 50 seconds for the JVM to warm up. For four minutes the existing pods take the full spike alone, and that's when users see errors. Meanwhile a downstream SaaS API starts returning 429s at a limit nobody knew about. Latency adds up and tails multiply. A request through six services pays six sets of network hops, serialisation and queueing. If a page calls 10 services in parallel, each with 1% of requests above 1 second, about 10% of page loads hit at least one slow call (1 − 0.99 10 ). See fan-out amplification and tail latency . The bottleneck moves. Scaling one service pushes load onto the next. Test the whole journey, not each service alone, then test individual services to find their limits. Shared resources hide behind service boundaries. Five services sharing one database, cache cluster or message broker all slow down together. Testing services one at a time won't show it. Timeouts and retries interact. If service A times out after 5 seconds and retries 3 times, and B does the same towards C, one slow call to C can become 9 calls. Check that timeouts get shorter as you go deeper, and that retries have budgets and jittered back-off. Distributed tracing is close to essential here. See reading a trace waterf

d: A free browser game about surviving Black Friday traffic. Add servers, caching, a CDN, read replicas, a checkout queue and a rate limiter, and keep p95 latency and errors inside your SLO without blowing the budget.
x: Games · Capacity planning Your shop has five waves of traffic coming, from a quiet Tuesday to the Black Friday peak. Build the setup that keeps p95 under 800 ms and errors under 1% , without blowing the budget. Wave 1 of 5 Normal Tuesday ❤️❤️❤️ Score 0 Traffic 0 req/s (bots incl.) p95 latency 0 ms SLO 800 ms Errors 0% SLO 1% Cost $0/h budget $6/h Orders 0 this wave traffic p95 SLO During a wave, new servers take 25 s to warm up, the way real instances do. Between waves, changes are instant. Keys: P pause, + / − servers, Enter start the next wave. Get ready It's a toy, but every effect in it is a real one you'll meet in a load test: Queueing: latency grows like 1 / (1 − utilisation). At 50% busy it barely moves; at 90% it's ten times the idle time. That's why you need headroom . Caching and the CDN take load off the database and the app tier. Checkouts can't be cached, so they always reach the database. Connections: connections in use = queries per second × query time ( Little's law ). Add app servers without a pooler and you can run the database out of connections . Autoscaling lag: new servers take time to start. If your traffic jumps in seconds, autoscaling alone is too late. Scale before the sale. Queues and rate limits: a checkout queue turns a database overload into a wait instead of an error, and a rate limiter keeps bots from using the capacity your customers need. Your real system has its own numbers. The only way to know them is to measure: a peak-readiness load test

Answer both here, then copy a k6 scenario sized for it. 🔒 Runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere. 1. Forecast the peak Daily volume → busiest hour → busiest minute. 2. Size the infrastructure Requests per second → cores, pods, DB connections. 3. Size the test Throughput → virtual users and a k6 scenario. Step 1 and 2 Start with orders (or sign-ins, searches, payments) per day. Replace the CPU cost with a number measured in a load test as soon as you have one. This calculator needs JavaScript. Step 3 Take the peak from step 1 as the target throughput. The calculator applies Little's Law and writes the k6 arrival-rate scenario for you. This calculator needs JavaScript. How it works The number of users in a system equals how fast they arrive times how long each one stays: virtual users = throughput × (response time + think time) 50 iterations/s × (0.8 s + 5 s) = 290 users That's for a closed model (a fixed pool of users with think time). An arrival-rate test (k6's constant-arrival-rate ) fixes the throughput instead, so it keeps the pressure on when the system slows down, which is what real traffic does. Traffic is never spread evenly. Retail often sees 15–30% of a day's orders in the busiest hour, and the busiest minute inside that hour runs another 2–3× above the hour'
